utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to greet all and everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Mr. Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are Monday, 15th of May, 2006. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom. I don't think you need to introduce yourselves because I think they are all the same people present this afternoon. We shall resume with witness testimonies this afternoon, but before that, a few housekeeping matters I'd like to address. First of all, time issues. I think we had an example of this last week. The Judges have decided that when the hearing is due to finish at a quarter to 2, we shall stop the person who is speaking at quarter to 2. We cannot overstep our time for several reasons. As you know, there are a lot of people working and helping this Chamber. There are security guards, there are staff members working for the Trial Chamber, and the interpreters. When we finish at quarter to 2, everybody must understand that all these people have started working at 9.00 in the morning and sometimes some of them have been there two hours before already, so we cannot overstep our time and cannot go beyond quarter to 2. The lawyer who has the floor at that time must keep an eye on the clock and that is the reason why the clock is up there in the courtroom; so that everybody can check the time. And make sure that the questions fit into the appropriate time frame. The Judges never like to cut a lawyer when he or her is speaking. It's always a rather tricky question, but sometimes it is important that people stick to the allotted time. There is also another issue of a technical nature. Sometimes there is another hearing in the courtroom afterwards and 30 minutes are required to change the videotapes or audiotapes. So it is most important to finish the hearing at quarter to 2 so that the next hearing can start on time. So I would ask all of you to be as disciplined as possible and make sure, given these requirements, that the time you spent or the time speaking is something which you clearly keep in check. We cannot go beyond our allotted time and therefore it is most important to be -- to keep this in check. This is something we wanted to share with you and we wanted to inform you about the decision we have taken. Now, as far as last week is concerned, the expert report by Mr. Donia, the Trial Chamber has decided to admit this report into evidence. Registrar, could you please give us a number for this expert report. I think, if I remember correctly, the number should be P 9356. I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This report has been admitted under the exhibit number you have mentioned. [In English] This report is admitted under the reference P 09536. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Secondly, because we ran out of time last week, I had to interrupt Mr. Praljak who was putting his questions to the witness. I would like to ask the Defence team - I think it's Mr. Jonjic - who was due to ask for some of his exhibits or documents to be admitted into evidence. So he has the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On Friday, because we didn't have enough time, I had to put off my request that the following exhibits be tendered: 5D 01026, 5D 01046, and 5D 01050. Those are the documents that were shown the witness, and if I may just say one more sentence, this morning -- of course, it's too late now since the Trial Chamber has taken its decision with respect to the report by Witness expert Donia -- I had a request asking that those findings should not be admitted into evidence and, if they are subsequently adopted, that when the Trial Chamber comes to assess and appraise its value, they should bear in mind that Dr. Donia demonstrated that he did not have the knowledge of elementary facts. In addition, he said that he had no knowledge about how the banovina of Croatia was first created and that he knew nothing about the changes of the -- in the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 20th century. He demonstrated that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, as far as the tendering into evidence of these three documents is concerned, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three documents are tendered into evidence under following numbers: [In English] 5D 01026, 5D 01046, 5D 01050. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as tendering into evidence of the expert report is concerned, I would like to tell all and everyone that if a report is tendered, this does not mean that the Trial Chamber deems that this report does have a probative value or that the exhibits have a probative value. All of this has to be checked out against other information, namely other expert reports, other expert evidence, and it is only at the end of the day that all of this will be assessed by the Bench. So you need not worry, it's not because the report is admitted that everything is set in stone. As you know, there will be other experts who will come to testify, other witnesses that will come and testify, there will be your own witnesses that will come and testify, so what is said today may change over time. So this is a golden rule which this Trial Chamber applies and which other Trial Chambers also apply. So you will have ample time to talk about the banovinas again, if you so wish when other witness will come to testify and when your own expert witness will come to testify. Mr. Jonjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I omitted to include one exhibit that was also shown to the witness. It is the description of the SS Division members, and that was document number 5D 01041. So might that be tendered into evidence as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right. This document got forgotten. Registrar, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is a Defence Exhibit which will be admitted under the following number: [In English] 5D 01041. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are still talking about expert reports. So the Prosecutor told us last week that as one of its witnesses could not come and testify, the Prosecution was going to call an expert witness earlier than expected. So the expert witness Mr. Tomljanovich should come and testify on Wednesday and Thursday. And this will be the examination-in-chief. The Defence counsel had -- the Defence teams had asked us to postpone the testimony of this witness to September. Mr. Sahota, who is here, did not have time but he was supposed to get back to us and give us his point of view, and let us know whether there were any confidentiality issues because this witness is an employee of the Tribunal and works for the Office of the Prosecutor. Now the question was raised whether during the examination-in-chief -- between the examination-in-chief and the month of September the Prosecution could use this time and prepare the witness for a number of answers he could give and when questions were put to him by the Defence team. The Prosecution did state that they would do nothing of the sort. In the meantime, we have been told that this witness may be called to testify in September. Mr. Sahota said he would let us know what his point of view was, and he's had ample time and he's had all the weekend to think about it. So, Mr. Sahota, what is your position on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have spoken to my colleagues on the Defence benches, and we agree that no objection will be taken in principle to this witness dividing his testimony in two installments. However, we would like the Court to consider issuing a caution or warning to the witness before he retires, having given his evidence-in-chief, asking him not to discuss his testimony in any form with any other individual. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sahota. In addition, we had one unanswered question which we didn't settle. Pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, when an expert report is actually recorded, the Defence as a general rule has one month in which to state its position. Either the Defence accepts the reports or if it wishes to cross-examine the witness, it can also challenge the quality of the witness or the relevance of the report. Given that this report has been recorded and given to the Registry on the 10th of May, the Defence would have until the 10th of June to state its position, but as one of the witnesses that was called to testify cannot come, the Prosecution has had to put this witness testimony forward and therefore the Defence has not had enough time to submit its filings. So this may raise a particular issue. If the Defence can file their written submission by the 15th of June, because a -- they will need 30 days. And the Defence will also have ample time to prepare its cross-examination. The Trial Chamber has accepted the fact that the cross-examination can take place in September. To sum up: The six Defence counsel will have the possibility or you can address us your submissions pursuant to Rule 94 bis before the 15th of June, and in the meantime, on Wednesday, we can hear this witness and it will be the direct examination of this witness and the Defence counsel will have a few months to prepare the cross-examination of the witness. Does the Defence team have anything to say about this? If the Defence team has nothing to say, I shall continue addressing the matter of expert reports. I shall give you the floor, Mr. Scott. Just let me finish and I'll give you the floor. I had drawn the attention of the Prosecution on the following during the Status Conference: I had indicated that between the beginning of the trial and the summer recess that we would have very little time, and that it would be better to call only one witness, one expert witness. The expert witness was in fact Mr. Donia, it so happens, and you couldn't organise it any other way. You happen to be calling another expert witness. Why not? But a third expert report has come in last week. So I would like to ask the Prosecution the following question: Do you intend to call this expert witness to testify on the 12th of July? This is a tall task for the Defence team because it has to prepare the cross-examination of the expert witness who is going to come to testify on Wednesday, the Defence team has to prepare the cross-examination of all other witnesses also, and if in addition there is a third expert witness who is also coming to -- calling to testify, maybe this is a little bit much. Is it really necessary to call this third expert witness before the 12th of July? Mr. Scott, I think you wanted to take the floor. Perhaps you can answer all of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, good afternoon. Let me start with the last question: No, there is no intention to call a third expert between now and the summer recess. It was simply a matter of disclosure. So the Defence have plenty of time to plan for the future, but there is no intention to call that witness prior to the summer recess. The other matter that I rose to my feet concerning a moment ago was concerning Mr. Tomljanovich. Your Honour, I raised last week when this issue came up whether the -- essentially, whether the Chamber would entertain the notion of a rule in this particular set of circumstances by which Mr. Tomljanovich would not be essentially, if you will, barred from having communication with the Prosecution, or you might use the word "sequestered," until such time as his cross-examination had begun, because that, of course, is the normal time when, once Defence starts putting questions to a witness, then the question arises, or the concern arises that there should be no opportunity for the Prosecution to influence the witness's potential answers once the cross-examination begins. As I indicated last week, obviously cross-examination now won't begin until sometime later, and there is no risk or prejudice that can arise from the Prosecution attempting to influence the witness since the cross-examination has not started yet. Having thought about this further over the weekend, Your Honour, I think I must press the Chamber, with all respect, to apply a rule in this case which would not in any way prevent the Prosecution from having continuing contact with Mr. Tomljanovich between the time that he finishes his direct examination and the time that he begins his cross-examination. And from among other reasons are this, Your Honour: Mr. Tomljanovich is a member of the Prosecution team. We work with him on a number of items, on a given day on a week-to-week basis. Some of these matters are so closely related I do not want to raise the possibility of someone making an allegation that we've spoken to him inappropriately on something that might be interpreted to be so closely related to his testimony that someone is going to raise the allegation that we have talked to him about his testimony. As Your Honours can see from his expert report, he talks about many, many aspects of the case, many dimensions of the case, and any number of which can conceivably come up in the course of any set of daily discussions about the case in general, about some other preparation of some other aspect of the case, et cetera. So under these particular circumstances, Your Honours, I would -- I don't think the Prosecution can go forward with putting Mr. Tomljanovich on the witness stand unless we can have a ruling and understanding that there will be no bar -- no caution, no bar, to the Prosecution continuing to speak with -- and work with Mr. Tomljanovich, because we work with him on a daily basis, until the cross-examination actually begins, albeit in September or whenever, and, of course, at that time, of course, no contact. But in the meantime -- in the interim time period, Your Honour, I do not think it is workable and I think it raises the opportunity for mischief, frankly, and allegations being made against the Prosecution that something has been said that someone will characterise as related to Mr. Tomljanovich's testimony. So I would ask the Court -- I'm asking the Court for a ruling that that -- any such caution or sequestration order not take affect until Mr. Tomljanovich's cross-examination begins. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, but as far as this particular point is concerned, before giving the floor to Mr. Karnavas, the Bench have discussed it. As far as we are concerned, we don't see any impediment to this but we should mention the fact that there is no question that you or Mr. Mundis discuss with this expert witness who works with you on other topics, that you discuss his report, and the answers he has provided to your questions during his examination-in-chief. Of course, you can talk to him about the weather and other cases and whatever; you name it. That, of course, you can do. But there is no question of you telling him, "I have asked you such and such a question. You have answered in such a way. During the cross, you will have to provide a different answer." This would be a contempt, of course, and nobody would even think of it. And I think all attorneys and lawyers have understood it this way. Mr. Karnavas, you would like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, on this issue, and then I have other issues that perhaps we can raise at -- later on but before the next witness comes in. First, I'm sure that no one on the side of the Prosecution will attempt to influence the witness as to what to say on cross-examination and changing their statement. I take them at their bona fides. They are professional, so I don't see that as a problem. The problem I do see, however -- I'll slow down for the interpreters. The problem I do see, however, is where Mr. Tomljanovich gives his direct examination, we have other witnesses coming in, now Mr. Tomljanovich is used as a resource to assist the Prosecution with respect to other witnesses. Of course, all with a sense of tailoring, perhaps, their testimony to fit Mr. Tomljanovich's direct examination, and there lies the problem. Now my heart goes out to it these folks, but let's face it, this trial was supposed to start in February. In fact, when I first got in the case, it was last October. We just got this report last week. One might ask: Why did it take them so long? I don't want to go into perhaps there were reasons that they wanted to frustrate the Defence. I don't want to go there, but the bottom line is we just received it. And I can tell you right now, Your Honours, I am going to need five days, minimum, of cross-examination. I'm going to be asking for that. This is the entire Prosecution case with respect to Mr. Prlic. I desperately will need that time and I desperately will need the time to go over that report because Mr. Tomljanovich, unlike Mr. Donia, was pretty thorough in documenting his positions, and so we will need to go through all of that. So I think that the problem with Mr. Tomljanovich is that it was -- their tardiness in bringing their report to us. Now they wish to put him on because they need to fill a gap. Fine. If they want to hold off, that's fine too but the bottom line is you can't put the Defence in a position where we might be prejudiced. One other thing with respect to expert witnesses, because I think this is going to come up again. The last report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just interrupt you for a few minutes. I would just like to finish off with Mr. Tomljanovich. For the length of time you have asked for, we haven't discussed it yet and the Bench hasn't discussed it yet but we would let you know how much time you will have for your cross-examination. But you have just raised an issue which I had not thought of. You are telling us that this expert witness works together with the Prosecution and can also work with witnesses to be. This is a real issue. Mr. Scott, this expert witness, is he going to be working with you in this case? In other words, to prepare other witnesses? Or is he going to be disconnected until September from the -- from trial management and he will be working on other things? Because if he is preparing the testimonies to come, and preparing the next witness, then there can be a certain degree of interference. I had understood you to say that this expert witness was in broad terms working for the Prosecution but was not specifically working on this case. If he's one of your close associates who is helping you to prepare the case and the examination-in-chief, this may raise an issue. Could you please fill us in on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was largely the point that I was in fact trying to make and perhaps not well enough, in explaining the unworkability, the unworkability of having Mr. Tomljanovich separated from the team during this period of time. Your Honour, in light of these concerns that have been expressed and in light of these issues that have been raised, we will not call Mr. Tomljanovich on Wednesday and we will just delay his testimony to the future. That means, however, we will have no witnesses this week on Wednesday and Thursday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, at least in an adversarial system you are able to solve some problems. We will not hear this witness on Wednesday. Unfortunately, you cannot call another witness, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's impossible for us to make other arrangements that quickly, I'm afraid. We have worked very hard in the last week to find witnesses who can come. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Karnavas is now satisfied. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That gives me more time to make my record, Your Honour. As I was talking about experts, just to finish on that point, General Pringle's expert is dated -- he signed it on the 26th of March 2006. 26th March, 2006. We are into May right now, as I understand it. The question is: Why didn't we get this report earlier? Now, the Prosecution can say, well, maybe they weren't planning on calling him. Nonetheless, the problem is if they have an expert, they know they are going to use this expert, they have the report, it's a signed report by the expert, why are they waiting until the last moment to give it to us? It really poses a problem. It's a problem of fairness, it's a problem of equality of arms. It is virtually impossible for us to be doing all of these things at the same time; go through an expert's report, check all the footnotes, check the resources. These are experts that we need experts to look over the expert reports. That's how it's done. So I just mention this for -- perhaps, you know, it was an oversight, but -- perhaps this won't happen again, perhaps the Court may wish to issue an order. Next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, I think fair play is no mean virtue. The Defence team is asking you how come that a report dated the 26th of March was only recorded a few days ago. Is there some administrative reason for this or was it just a lack of fair play?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just lack of -- lack of attention to it, if you will, in the sense of inadvertence. It had not been displayed earlier. I'm not sure why this is a basis of complaint at this juncture. I've just indicated a few moments ago this witness will not be called until sometime next fall. I cannot imagine any possible prejudice to the accused. You know, believe it or not, the Prosecution is also working very, very hard and has many issues to deal with on a day-to-day basis. Mr. Pringle's report didn't go out earlier. We sent it out last week, fully knowing - fully knowing - that he would not be coming for some number of months. So I think the Defence has adequate time to prepare, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just respond to that because I think perhaps there is a different way of doing things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please, Mr. Karnavas. I think we've settled the issue. You have asked your question. The Prosecution has answered your question. Let's move on to another issue now, please. So which is the other issue you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But I'm coming back to this particular issue because in preparing for a Defence, Your Honour, you need to prepare it completely, not in snippets. That's my point. My next point was Mr. Donia. Obviously I'm highly disappointed that the report is coming in, albeit you're going to be giving it some weight at some other point of time, but I must express for the record certain concerns: One, there was the issue that we were not allotted sufficient time. This is an expert report. I can state on the record with full responsibility that this particular Defence team, my team alone, spent literally hundreds of hours preparing for Donia's cross-examination. We were limited to about 3 and a half hours. I was wondering over the weekend why am I preparing a case if I'm not going to be allowed to fully challenge each and every word that the report has in it? So I had to gut my cross-examination. It was very disjointed. I have here what I would like to put on the record, or make part of the record, on an ex parte basis, an outline of my cross-examination, ex parte in the sense that the Prosecution should not be able to have my theory or -- of how I was going to challenge Mr. Donia, since I wasn't allowed to cross-examine him on several areas. I don't know how to go about it but that's something to consider. Secondly with respect to Mr. Donia, I thought it was inappropriate, and I say this with all due respect but I cannot find any other word to describe it, but I thought it was inappropriate for a member of the Bench to comment to the witness that they found the report to be a good report when in fact the witness was still being -- hadn't been fully cross-examined by all the Defence. I can only assume that it was to comfort the witness. After all, the witness was under attack by the Defence for a day and a half, and so I think the comment was not meant in any particular fashion; however, from the Defence standpoint, I can assure that it generated a big deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the witness Mr. Donia came here to testify before this Trial Chamber, or rather, came to this Tribunal to testify eight times already. He testified in eight different trials. It's up to you to do what you wish. Of course you can challenge his work, report or his competence. But as I've told you previously, the fact that some expert report is tendered into evidence doesn't mean that the Trial Chamber will fully rely on it. In addition to that, you yourself have a chance to challenge that report in your submissions. When other witnesses come, you will have a chance to point out through these other witnesses precisely why in your view this report was bad. You can bring in your own expert witnesses who will testify differently. So please don't let this upset you, the fact that somebody said that this was a good report. Don't confuse the quality of report and quality work put in report and the probative value of a report. Please don't let yourself be upset about it. The second issue has to do with time. All of us would like to have more time available to us, however we are all faced with temporal limitations. We cannot give you an unlimited amount of time. When you cross-examined this witness, you used up about an hour and a half in dealing with questions which were perhaps interesting but, given that you were aware of the lack of time, you could have abbreviated your cross-examination. This is your strategy. This is your line of defence. You chose not to abbreviate it. But as the trial goes on, you will have an opportunity to challenge everything that this witness said. I'm reminding you once again that we are not here to decide about the history but, rather, to decide on relevant issues in this trial. Let me remind you that in the Blaskic judgement, the testimony of Dr. Donia was mentioned only in two footnotes, so please don't ignore this fact. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not ignoring the fact and I'm very cognizant and mindful of the special rules of evidence that we have here. I am. But for me to challenge, I cannot challenge through other witnesses if I don't have, for instance, the facilities or the means to hire experts in my case. There is a presumption that somehow we are going to be able to have these resources to challenge. And I raise this issue with Donia because when it comes to other witnesses, such as Tomljanovich, I dare say if strict limitations are placed, we are going to be faced with a quandary here: Can we serve the interests of the Security Council and the interests of justice in the same time? And I don't think that those are irreconcilable at this point, if we have a strict time line. Now, I had proposed that Donia not appear and his report not come in because I thought he's not relevant to the case, but I was overruled on that. But be that as it may, I take your point, Mr. President, but nonetheless, I do have an outline I would like to make part of the record with respect to Mr. Donia. The next thing is some -- that I wanted to bring up are some technical issues, just very briefly. There are some technical issues: No access to -- remote access to LiveNote, no remote access to exhibits. There is an issue with the 65 ter exhibits, 9.500 of them, technical issues that impact us. I just raise that because I'm hoping that the Trial Chamber will look into this, and of course, if we are fumbling on this end, it's only because we are trying to work with everybody else in resolving these issues. And I'm not blaming anyone, I'm just stating that for the record. Lastly, it goes to the next witness who is about to appear. I wanted to raise a couple of issues. One, we received today some witness information, a witness statement. It's not much, but nonetheless we received it today. I'm not going to belabour the point. Normally I would, but I'm not. There are two particular videos, that I'm aware of, at least. One is an interview taken by my client. Obviously, I have no objections to that entire interview coming in in its entirety, and if that was the -- if that's the only thing that comes in, I certainly have nothing to ask this witness. With respect to the other video, however, it's a montage, it's snippets of interviews of various people, including something taken out of context from my client. There is footage. There is all this dramatic language involved. We don't have the full and complete text of everyone who was interviewed. So, for instance, the late President Tudjman, we don't have the full text. Or Boban or Susak or the others. It's a montage, we believe -- or at least I believe, that there is no probative value to this video. It's only prejudicial. There is absolutely nothing from which you can draw from other than it's a something that is for public audience, it has a particular point of view, it's slanted, and it is certainly not evidence worthy of being in any Tribunal anywhere in the world. Therefore, I would move at this point in time that before the witness -- before we see this video, that the Prosecution put forward questions in order to establish a foundation as to why this video is worthy and then give us perhaps the opportunity to raise this issue again, but I move that the video not be shown, that it not be admitted, that it's inadmissible because it's more prejudicial than probative, and that if that video doesn't in, then obviously I have no real cross-examination at all to do. But if it does come in, then it puts us again back into that time frame situation. I would have to go and challenge virtually every sentence that this woman says on this video. And also, it puts me at a great disadvantage because I don't have the full transcript of the late President Tudjman or the late Susak or the late Boban to see in what context they were speaking when they made those remarks. In fact, we don't have a transcript at all of any of these folks, and there are other -- two other or three other or five other individuals that are questioned. We don't have transcripts for any one of them. So based on those reasons, we are being prejudiced, it shouldn't come in Your Honour, and we could save a lot of time by simply admitting the one full interview of my client and we can thank the young lady -- or the lady - I don't know how old she is - but we can thank her and she can go on her business. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Kovacic. I will give you the floor, but prior to that I would like to hear from Mr. Scoot. Mr. Karnavas raised a problem here, and if I understood him well, there are two videotapes that you intend to play. The Defence believes that there could be problems regarding something contained on one of the tapes because this is actually a montage, a videotape containing several different clips, and certain things have been taken out of context, because all of these clips were edited and then put together. So what is your intention? Do you intend to first examine the witness and then play the tape, or how do you intend to proceed regarding this? I see that it's going to be you, Mr. Mundis. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution was planning on laying a foundation, asking the witness precisely how it was that she came about to produce this film. It's basically a documentary, what we might call a documentary. She went, and she will explain to you how she went and interviewed people and shot video contemporaneously in the late autumn of 1993, how she had edited this together and produced this television show which was then aired on a British television network. We were planning on laying the foundation for that. It's not a lengthy foundation, but it's a foundation nevertheless. We would then ask the videotape be played. The issues raised by my learned colleague Mr. Karnavas go to weight and not to admissibility. That is, that the issues that he's put forward before you go to, again, the issue what weight you might give to that videotape. The items, the issues that he's raised concerning the bias, if you will, of the witness, to use a shorthand term for what Mr. Karnavas has described, that's clearly an issue for cross-examination. The witness can be cross-examined on any bias that she may have had. These are all issues, Your Honour, that can be addressed in cross-examination. And again, just because something is contained in a videotape doesn't mean that the Chamber will give it a great deal of weight. It's contextual. It goes to providing the Trial Chamber at this early stage in these proceedings with an overview. That's all it is, Mr. President. It's a 50-minute, 45-minute long documentary that was produced for British television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to ask the question: What's the relevance? And I guess I heard it: This is an overview. The title of it is "A Greater Croatia." Now, if that's not a result-oriented, you know, documentary, if you want to call it that, I don't know what is. I can assure you that when my client was approached and signed a waiver, he wasn't aware of the title of it, and that certainly wasn't the case, and I agree with my learned colleague Mr. Mundis that just about anything can come in and then we sort it out at the end, but here, I think one of the fundamental principles of keeping certain evidence out is whether it's more prejudicial than probative, and if it has no probative value -- and I suggest, Your Honours, it has zero probative value, and it doesn't give context, because when you see the video, it doesn't present a balanced point of view, so what kind of context does it give? And if they are going to lay a foundation through the witness, then I'd ask Your Honours that before we even see the video, that I would be permitted to do what they call a voir dire to pose questions to the witness specific to the issue of foundation. Not into contents but strictly issues of foundation and then you can make a determination as to whether the video should be played or not. I'm confident that when you see the video, and even if it's admitted, you're not going to give it any evidentiary value, or any weight. I'm confident of that. But I'm saying that I don't think that we should bringing in all this sort of inflammatory footage simply because it's convenient or because somehow it fits the Prosecution's theory. It's not a balanced documentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two sets of rules when it comes to video material. One type of video material is the one that can be introduced when the witness itself was a director or interviewed the person, and then that witness is expected to say well on such-and-such day, you taped this footage, or you interviewed this person, and this is how it is confirmed. So that's one way that this can be done. The other way is that sometimes video material is introduced into evidence even though we don't have the director, cameraman, or the journalist. However, this material is nevertheless relevant if it pertains to an event covered by the indictment. This is why it is relevant. As for its probative value, this is something that the Judges will decide upon after hearing both sides. We will decide on the probative value at the very end. In all trials, there are numerous video tapes that are tendered into evidence, or photographs, and then at the end, you will see that 5 per cent or less of them are actually relied upon. They are only sometimes mentioned in the footnotes. And it is only sometimes that they are relied upon. Mr. Karnavas, you touched upon the relevant issues. First of all, we haven't heard the witness, and second, we haven't seen the video material, so how are the Judges supposed to know this in advance? In addition to that, another judge would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are quite well aware of this, but it is important, that this is a professional Bench and we do not have a jury. So a jury might be impressed by seeing a video and are not able then to take a critical distance, but I hope you trust that these professional judges are able to look at the video and all the time think, "We'll see what it's worth."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's precisely. If I had a jury, if it was in front of a jury, I can see why they would want to sneak in something like that to prejudice and inflame the passions of the jury. But we don't. We have dispassionate judges. That's why I don't see why they would bring in something that has no value. That's precisely my point. I am fully confident of this Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Even though I agree with almost everything Mr. Karnavas said, but I don't think that actually he represents the entire Defence here, so I will also -- I would like to add two or three minor issues here. If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps I cut you off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's working now? [Interpretation] It seems to be working now. As for the expert witness Tomljanovich, I fully support everything said by the Defence of Mr. Prlic. I don't think I need to add anything there. However, in view of some questions raised by the Honourable Trial Chamber, I would like to say this as I don't know whether the Chamber is informed about this, based on the discussion. I remember, on the basis of reading some witness statements, witnesses who were called in and interviewed in this case. These were witnesses who were called here as suspects, called here and examined by the Prosecution, and Mr. Tomljanovich was present in a large number of such examinations. Based on what I heard from suspects and witnesses - and I think that this can be found in certain records that we received - Mr. Tomljanovich occasionally took a very direct part in such examinations. My question now is whether the role of Mr. Tomljanovich is limited to what was portrayed here by the Prosecution or is Mr. Tomljanovich so involved in the Prosecution work that it makes no difference whether one of the prosecutors will come to testify here or Mr. Tomljanovich himself. I'm not saying this is a completely identical situation but it is a fact that it is very, very close and it would be as though I proposed my co-counsel, Ms. Nika Pinter, as a witness here because she's been so involved in this case that she's obviously an expert here. And I don't think that I could do this in view of many formal, legal limitations. On the other hand, the Prosecution is proposing that one of their own, a member of their team, be called here to testify. I think this goes against some basic rules, safeguarding fairness of the trial. But we don't need to go into this now because this witness is not coming, after all, this week and perhaps we will be submitting our position in writing. As far as expert witness Tomljanovich is concerned, my formal proposal is that he not be allowed to come here to testify as expert witness and that, likewise, his expert report not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (redacted) The witnesses scheduled for the 22nd and 23rd. I'm not going to mention any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No names were shown in the transcript. Was that what you wanted to intervene about, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, actually, I'm just wondering if we need to be raising a number of administrative issues right now, given than we will have some time later this week that's now available because Mr. Tomljanovich will not be testifying, while at the same time we have a witness whose -- who was expecting to start her testimony at 2.15 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please go ahead, Mr. Kovacic, but speed up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. Here in the courtroom on Thursday last week, the Prosecution gave us a new calendar. It caught us unprepared. We were unable to verify it. I wasn't going to object about these witnesses coming one day before they come, and today was the first day when I was able to object because today was the first day that I was able to look at the calendar. So these witnesses scheduled for Monday and Tuesday next week, 22nd and 23rd, are not listed in the second table where we have more detailed information about the witnesses coming before summer recess. They were put on the list of viva voce witnesses, the annex that came in with the pre-trial brief, but they were not put on the other list. So a week before they are scheduled to come, we are being told that these witnesses are coming and we were not expecting them before summer recess. So this caught us unprepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, just two sentences concerning the expert witness Tomljanovich. I believe that the jurisprudence of this Court as well as the Court in Rwanda is telling us that the person employed in the OTP cannot be considered a biased witness a priori and should not be banned on the basis of that. However, I think that there are plenty of cases showing that a person working for the Prosecution and involved in the case can be viewed with -- more thoroughly. I think that there is bias with this witness, and I agree with what my colleagues before me said, both Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Kovacic. I think that this witness is a biased witness and we should view him as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are going to discuss this among the Judges. We have two more issues to discuss but we will go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume the hearing. Good afternoon, Madam. You have been called to testify by the Prosecution. Before you read the solemn declaration, I would like to ask you a number of questions to -- for you to introduce yourself. Could you give us your first name, last name, your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Belinda Giles. My place of birth is Paris, France. And your other question was? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9th of the 6th, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am currently a student. I was a television producer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have you testified before on the events that took place in ex-Yugoslavia before an international Tribunal or a national Tribunal or is this the first time you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you go ahead and read the solemn declaration now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. Please be seated. As I said a moment ago, Madam, you're now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, which is sitting to your right. And this will be the first stage during the afternoon. And afterwards, the Defence teams and the Defence counsel of the accused sitting to your left will be asking you questions. There are quite a lot of them. A few of them will be asking you questions on the basis of what we call in common law the cross-examination, and you will be able to see that the types of questions will be different than those asked you by the Prosecution. The Judges sitting in front of you, the four judges opposite you, can, if they deem necessary in the interests of justice, also ask you questions. If you have any difficulty of any kind, please let us know. We are here to help you. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, ask the question to be reformulated, asked again. And if you need some time to think before you answer, please do so, so that we can hear your testimony in the best possible conditions. Once we have started the examination-in-chief, we will be working for one and a half hours and then we'll take a break to give you a chance to rest for about 20 minutes and then we'll reconvene and we will finish today by 7 p.m. Having said that, I'm going to turn to the Prosecution to give them the floor. It is Mr. Mundis. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Giles.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You answered in response to a question of the Presiding Judge that you had formerly been a television producer. Can you please tell us what that job entails.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: In my case, I was an independent television producer, working for my own company, and my job was to come up with ideas which I then sold to broadcasters, in the U.K. primarily. And if they were interested in the subjects that I proposed, these broadcasters would then give me money to go and fund a project that I would then make which would then be broadcast on the appropriate channel that had funded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the day-to-work work of a television producer. What exactly do television producers do?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, television producers work -- I mean, particularly independent television producers work across a variety of different tasks. As I've just explained, it's -- there is a lot of development of new ideas. Once an idea has been sold to a broadcaster, it's a matter of putting the ideas that you have suggested into reality by researching the project, then filming it, then editing it and preparing it for broadcast on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Giles, of these various constituent parts of the television production business - that is filming, editing, preparing for broadcast, researching - how much of that did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, again, there are no hard and fast rules but I would normally do everything, every part, or certainly have a major role in every part. I might have a cameraman who would shoot the actual pictures but I would almost invariably be there to direct the pictures and make sure that we had got the right material that I needed. I would have an editor who would actually technically put the material together but it would be me who would be in charge of determining in what way those were put together, the script; you know, all the details that ended up on the final -- on the screen in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who would conduct the interviews?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Again, it depends, but I would often conduct the interviews. It depends in what circumstances you're working with. You can be working with a well-known television presenter who would do the interviews, it can be the director who can do the interviews; it just varies according to project.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of training or education did you have to enter this profession?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I started my career in television in the BBC. I was what's called a graduate trainee, which means that I had a degree in history and I applied to the BBC to join them on a graduate trainee programme for two years. I started with 12 other people who had similar degrees, not only in history but across the range of academic subjects, and I was trained on the job as a researcher initially, then as an assistant producer, and then I became a producer and a director.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at the BBC?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I was there from 1979 to 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you begin doing in 1986?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I then became a freelance producer, working for various different companies, and in 1988, I would say, I set up my own production company to do my own projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the name of your production company?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It was called Sole Purpose Productions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many persons were employed by Sole Purpose Productions?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, initially, it was just me, but by the end -- I closed the company four years ago. By the end, we had about 50 people working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What are some of the projects or films that were produced by Sole Purpose Productions?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We did a whole range of stuff across that time, from documentary to historical things, to political, foreign affairs. I suppose if there is one thing I particularly majored on was projects about the former Yugoslavia. I did eight films in all about the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you do so many films about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I became very interested in it, and I went there initially at the beginning of the war to make a film about refugees, and I just became very absorbed by the whole -- the politics, the war; everything. The people. It was -- it became a passion for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- what were these people, the first film that you've told us about, refugees, who were these people and refugees from where or from whom?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, I was asked by the BBC to make a film about the nature of suffering and I made a film really based all over Bosnia and Croatia, not in Serbia at that time, just about what the experience of leaving your home, losing everything, was like. It wasn't a political film at all. It was an emotional film about -- about what people were undergoing at that very time. It was in late 1992, so it was sort of -- it was at the height of the cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "cleansing," who was doing this cleansing?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: At that point, it was the Serb cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were the victims?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: The victims, we had -- we featured a lot of Croatian victims. A lot of Croatian victims. I would say probably a majority of Croatian victims, actually, who had been cleansed out of Northern Bosnia and Central Bosnia, and also Croats who had actually, you know, obviously had to leave their own areas in Croatia. And there were also -- we featured quite a lot of Muslim refugees who were at that time being cleansed out of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Giles, what was the second film that you made about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: The second film was a film called "A Greater Croatia," which we made for channel 4 television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us not about this film yet, because I'll come back to that, but about the other six films you made about the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I made two films about the International War Crimes Tribunal here. One was about the first case, Dusko Tadic, about how he had become the first person to stand trial at The Hague, the sort of judicial system that had been set up to try him, and how he came to be the first defendant, and his own background in Bosnia. I then did another film about the -- after the Tadic trial, examining the process and how it had been carried out. I did a film about the Serbs and the nature of the Serbs called "The Corridor." It was at a time when sort of the maps were yet again being redrawn and it broadly focused on the route, it was a sort of road movie, from Belgrade through to Knin. And I did another film, again with a collaboration of the International War Crimes Tribunal, following from day one the excavation of the mass grave at Vukovar, which went from, as I say, day 1 through to DNA identification in the morgue. That was a long film that won many awards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return now to the film, "A Greater Croatia." Can you tell us how the idea for that film was formulated?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, in the first film that I have described, the one about refugees, we had been to Herzegovina and I think we had also spent some time in Zagreb. It was an area that we were, as I say, very interested in by that time. And it was not me that came up with the idea. It was my colleague, Paulette Farsides, who had a great -- who had been a journalist out there, and she suggested that we look at what was going on in Herzegovina as the mini-state of Herceg-Bosna was being set up. And we sold this idea to channel 4, to look at the sort of complexity of whether the mini-state that was being set up was really for the Croats of Bosnia generally or whether it was for the Croats of Bosnia in Herzegovina, and to look at that tension, and to look also at the fact that whilst the Serbs were kind of being targeted as the people who were doing the real really bad things in Yugoslavia, whether the Croats were getting away with similar sorts of crimes whilst the world's media wasn't able to focus on another element of this very complicated conflict. So we put this forward to channel 4 as a proposal and they immediately went for it and asked us to leave. I think we left within a week. As you can imagine, it was a fast-breaking story. There was a lot going on at this period. So we went out there pretty quickly to start filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the filming process for "A Greater Croatia"? Where did you go? Whom did you interview?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We spent some time in Zagreb. We interviewed President Tudjman and we interviewed Mr. Susak, who was then the defence minister. We also interviewed some people. We interviewed, I remember, Bilandzic and Slaven Letica, who were people who had been part of the sort of Tudjman entourage, particularly, I think, Bilandzic, but had fallen out with him and were quite revealing about the intentions of some elements of the Croatian government, I think particularly President Tudjman. We then travelled down to the region, to Herzegovina, and we filmed all over the place but mostly in Capljina where we had been before on the project, the previous project, and we had come to know the mayor and so he gave us access to places that we wouldn't have had otherwise. And shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: And we also went to Mostar. We went to both West Mostar and East Mostar. I went to West Mostar under the auspices of the UN, in an armoured convoy with the Spanish Battalion that were stationed there at the time. And I went to -- sorry, I went to East Mostar in that way, and I went to West Mostar in a -- just an ordinary van. We went two or three times to film there, and -- yes, that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you first go to Herzegovina to produce this film?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, the exact date I'm not completely sure because it was around the first or the second week of November of 1993. And I'm pretty sure that the first time I went into Mostar itself was the day that the bridge fell, because obviously there was a lot of talk about the bridge, and it had already had -- did have quite a symbolic value, and I remember when we arrived in Mostar, the news was already out the bridge has fallen, the bridge has fallen, and it was a great shock to everybody, although there were very few people on the streets, but I remember that, that it was a great shock to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Ms. Giles, just for the record, when you refer to the bridge, which bridge are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I mean the old bridge, the old Ottoman bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to produce this film or create this film?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Again, I cannot be completely sure, but I think we were in the region -- we also went to Sarajevo, and it was very complicated to go to Sarajevo because we had to sort of fly out and fly in with the UN. I think the whole thing, we were there for probably three weeks in all, maybe a bit longer, maybe four weeks, and then we came home and we had to put it together probably in another three weeks. So it was probably a maximum of six to eight weeks, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Ms. Giles, when you say "we," who worked for you on this project?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: There was me, I was the director, and then I had Paulette Farsides, who I've already mentioned, who had had the idea for the programme. I had a cameraman called David Bailey, and a local translator who was from Zagreb, who was a colleague from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who did you interview, if anyone, during the time period you were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I only interviewed Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the circumstances under which this interview was arranged?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't be precise about it. I have a feeling that it was arranged through the office of Mate Boban, who we had also interviewed in Grude, but it may have been the other way around. It may have been that we interviewed Mr. Prlic first and then Mr. Boban, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about how that interview started?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't really remember how the interview started. I remember we turned up and Mr. Prlic welcomed us. He was very easy. He wanted to do the interview in English, which was helpful for me because it's always easier interviewing someone in your own language. We turned up in his office, and it was away from the front line, and I was very frightened by being in Mostar at all. I can't really remember any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the three- to four-week period that you spent putting the film together, following the time you were in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I remember it being a very complicated -- it's a very complicated story, as I'm sure you will understand, to convey to an audience in Britain who were already extremely confused by Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Serbs. All the details were very dense, and we were trying to make this even more complicated story, where you have funny names like Herceg-Bosna coming in, and Herzegovina. People had just got used to the idea of Bosnia and Serbia and Croatia, and what was this new entity? And trying to get that across and trying to explain the complexities of the story, as I said already; the whole idea of the Croats of middle -- Central Bosnia being sacrificed for the sort of interests of Herzegovina. I remember having a lot of discussions about how we could actually put this across in a way that was understandable to a lay audience, and structuring it so that it had a kind of dynamic appeal that would interest an audience. It was very difficult in what was really a very short time, because channel 4 wanted to get it out. It was a story that was happening then and there and they didn't want it to become outdated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Ms. Giles, who worked on this phase, that is the final assembly and putting together of the movie?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It was me and my colleague, Paulette Farsides, who I've already mentioned, and we had an editor - I cannot remember her name - but she, as I think I've already explained, editors play a part in the editorial process because their input is valuable but she is really in charge of the technology to make sure the pictures and the sound work rather than the sort of editorial structure. So the editorial structure was me and my colleague and, of course, the editors at channel 4 who had the -- who we were doing the work for, so they had their input as well at certain stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when "A Greater Croatia" aired on channel 4?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I would say that it was before Christmas. I would say it was the middle of December but I may be completely wrong. It may have been early in January, but I think it was -- I think it was the end of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point in time we would ask that the film "A Greater Croatia" be played in court. It has been previously marked, I believe, as P 07437. My case manager reminds me to say this, it is in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "On Dispatches tonight, the unreported story of the Bosnian war. How the Croatian government has shared in the carve-up of Bosnia just as it always intended, and how it's got away with it. Tonight, as the Croats meet to talk peace with their former Muslim allies in Vienna, Dispatches reveals the secret protocols that betrayed those same Muslims. That's Dispatches: How the Croats have created a brand new country in Bosnia just for themselves and how the West has turned a blind eye to a Greater Croatia. "Capljina, a town in Herceg-Bosna, a new country few people have ever heard of but a country that's determined to put itself on the European map. Herceg-Bosna is the mini-state that Croats have carved out of what was once Bosnia and now Capljina's mayor, Pero Markovic, can look forward to a brave new world. "[Interpretation] In the future, I hope that together with the world, with the help of the world, and all those who want to experience life in a democracy, we are part of Europe and we want to be like them. We must rebuild our lives. We want to educate ourselves. And we must get ready to take our place in Europe, where we belong. "[In English] Before Herceg-Bosna can take its place in Europe towns like Capljina have a lot of work to do. Not just repairing the damage caused by the Serb attack 18 months ago but also removing the traces of a second, more chilling battle. Capljina seems to be getting back to normal but scratch beneath the surface and everything has changed. One in four of the town's population has left. They didn't choose to go. Six months ago, Capljina was sealed off by the militia, street by street, block by block, a quarter of the town's people were loaded into buses and driven away. They were all Muslims. This was the final step in a campaign of persecution which began when Muslim cafes and shops were looted and destroyed. Herceg-Bosna has not emerged by accident. The setting up of this state is the realisation of a long-term plan. Today all the players in the Capljina football team are Croats. They play beneath the Croatian chequerboard flag. The story of how the Serbs carved out their chunk of Bosnia is well known. The Croats have now done the same, but their game plan has been overlooked. Herceg-Bosna owes its existence to one man - Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman. For him, the making of a Croat state on Bosnian land has been a personal obsession, an obsession which drove him to bang the final nail into Bosnia's coffin. Tudjman has built this state on concentration camps, ethnic cleansing, torture, starvation, all executed by his henchman, Mate Boban. "The Croats were the smallest group in Bosnia, fewer than a fifth of the population, but they've always dominated the barren landscape of Herzegovina. Herzegovinians looked to the Croatian capital, Zagreb, rather than Sarajevo, as their capital. This rocky terrain bred the fascist Ustashas of World War II. To this day, Herzegovinians display a virulent strain of Croatian nationalism. It's a philosophy of intolerance, a lot of prejudice. They hate state as an institution. They hate texts. They hate everything. They need only space and territory. "After World War II poverty drove tens of thousands of Herzegovinians to abandon this infertile land. In emigre communities abroad their nationalist fervour only deepened. They dreamed of their region becoming part of Croatia. It was a dream shared by Croatian president Franjo Tudjman. He always believed that Croatia had an historic claim in Bosnia. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Tudjman's obsession with Croatian claims in Bosnia runs deep. In 1991, he meets his arch enemy, Serbian president, Slobodan Milosevic, for secret discussions. Even though Serbia is threatening to invade Croatia, Tudjman is still happy to talk about their one common interest, a carve-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Two eye witnesses of this meeting in Karadjordjevo can now reveal the real agenda. "That was never… in the mass-media and no complete information about that was ever given. Hence, they were secret talks. But the mass-media portrayed them as being talks between Serbia and Croatia on unresolved problems between the two states. Nothing more. Moreover, it was denied… the rumors and stories going around and all the speculations that it was about Bosnia were denied. It was denied. "[In English] There were several maps on the table, I guess, and the idea was more or less close to the recent ideas on Bosnia-Herzegovina, that -- that means either to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina into ten or 15 units or in three semi-independent states. "Did the Muslims attend this meeting? "No, absolutely. Absolutely no. [No interpretation] "Tudjman has swept to power on a nationalist ticket but most of his advisers opposed his ambitions in Bosnia. However, Tudjman is an autocrat who listens only to the people who agree with him. He found unconditional support elsewhere. Emigre Herzegovinians had poured money into Tudjman's election campaign. They were confident he would promote their nationalist ambitions not only in Croatia but also in Bosnia. The most prominent is Gojko Susak. Until four years ago, Susak was a pizza parlour entrepreneur in Toronto. Now he's the defence minister of Croatia. "President had a view on Bosnia-Herzegovina long before we met. He was very explicit, and that at the very first public speech when he came to the US and Canada, that's when I first met him. His politics were on known Bosnia-Herzegovina were defined. They do coincide with my view of Bosnia-Herzegovina in many ways. "There is a double game between the two. At personal level, Mr. Susak is a kind of Tudjman's slave. He accepts every decision made by Mr. Tudjman, so his non-existing personality at personal level, but in political sense, Mr. Tudjman sometime or even at present time, very often exhibits political -- Mr. Susak's political philosophy. "But for the Croats of Sarajevo and the rest of Bosnia, Tudjman's ambitions were dangerous. The Herzegovinans, who number only 200.000, had always lived together, but 600.000 other Croats were scattered in mixed communities throughout Bosnia. They couldn't easily be disentangled. These Croats already had their own leadership in Sarajevo. "[No interpretation] "[In English] But unknown to Kljuic, the president of all Croats was already preparing the ground for a division of Bosnia. Even as he makes his first presidential visit to the Croats of Sarajevo, Tudjman is secretly backing a small group of extremist Herzegovina politicians who are plotting a separate Croat state in Bosnia. But he reveals nothing of his true intentions to this audience. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Dispatches has obtained the signed secret protocol produced by that group in November 1991. It confirms decisions reached with Tudjman in Zagreb. It declares Croatian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina must finally start a decisive and active policy, which is supposed to lead us to our centuries' long dream: A common Croatian state. They'll show Europe and the world which regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina are Croatian and where our future lies. "The document lays out the real plan. First, a Croat province in Bosnia is declared, next any Croat leaders who support a united Bosnia must be removed. Within two months of the meeting, with Tudjman's backing, the separatists force Kljuic to resign. Herzegovinan Mate Boban, whose main claim to fame was a spell in jail for black marketeering, is installed as the new leader. A plan is underway. Boban moves the Croat power base to this factory in his home town of Grude in Herzegovina. "This town with just two main streets and no town square takes the place of sophisticated Sarajevo. The next stage is simple: Boban sets up a separate Croat army in Bosnia, the HVO. March 1992, Croats vote with Muslims for independence. The Serbs rebel and war breaks out. As the Serbs cut a swathe through Bosnia, Croatia steps in to help the beleaguered state. Tudjman signs a military alliance with Bosnian President Izetbegovic to fight the Serbs. Tudjman knows that the mainly Muslim Bosnian government has little choice but to rely on Croatia. This serves his purpose. "[No interpretation] "[In English] He thought that Muslims would join Croatia, that was -- I mean, that was a second thought behind his political mind. "Croats and Muslims link up to fight the Serbs. Many Muslims join the HVO, which is better prepared than government forces. "[No interpretation] "[In English] But once the alliance has halted the Serb advance, Boban moves to the next stage of the master plan. He declares that the Bosnian government is dissolved and announces that the HVO has taken over in all areas unoccupied by the Serbs. The strains in the alliance are obvious. "Well, superficially they were working together as partners. There was a coalition which had taken them through the referendum on independence, and on the face of it, you thought that you were dealing with the Croats and the Muslims versus the Serbs. It was not many weeks before I realised that this was not a true coalition. "[No interpretation] "[In English] But to the HVO's supposed partner in the alliance, the takeover seems far from temporary. Ivan Negovetic is a Croat who enlisted not in the HVO but in the Bosnian government army. "[No interpretation] "[In English] To tighten its grip across Bosnia, the HVO has to weaken its alliance partner. Dispatches has obtained official documents which show the restrictions the HVO placed on the Bosnian army. In many areas, supposedly under joint control, the HVO requisitions all industry, power supplies, and transport. All consignments of weapons to the Bosnian army need to pass through Croatia and Herzegovina. At each check-point, some of the consignment is hived off and most of the weapons end up in HVO hands. In Grude alone, 37 trucks of weapons intended for the defence of Sarajevo are halted and plundered. "[No interpretation] "[In English] The alliance starts to collapse. In some areas Bosnian forces are disarmed and expelled by the Croats. In others, they fight back and push the HVO out. "Serb aggression becomes a distant memory as Croats and Muslims begin a scramble for territory. They fight each other with the bitterness born of betrayal. Bosnia is dead. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Tudjman and Boban are already rewriting history. They planned to seize power across Bosnia but the Bosnian army stopped them. Now the official Croat line blames Muslims for destroying the alliance. "[No interpretation] "[In English] As the alliance crumbled, Western negotiators failed to react to the Croat territorial ambitions. The Croats have taken care to pose as the reasonable party in the Bosnian conflict. "They were the weakest group because they are the smallest group and I think they were quite clever politically to decide that by and large they would go along with the negotiators. They would be the reasonable party, that was in their interest to be that. And I think that was a clever strategy. "That strategy is about to pay dividends. Now the peace negotiators are poised to give the Croats the green light for the final dismantling of Bosnia. "December 1992, Geneva. As the Vance-Owen peace plan is being drafted, the Croats are tightening their grip throughout their planned mini-state Herceg-Bosna. The plan divides Bosnia into ten provinces but it appears to ignore Mate Boban's obvious territorial ambitions, ambitions which the negotiators knew only too well. "One was well aware that they had been pursuing their own agenda way before the Vance-Owen plan was announced. That was, we were very conscious of it. The Herceg-Bosna question was a constant issue between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman. So there was nothing -- there was no surprises by then. We were fully aware of what was their private agenda. "Even so, the Croats see the Vance-Owen peace plan as an endorsement of their private agenda. Two of the provinces have a clear Croat majority, the third is half Muslim. Boban claims this province for himself. He insists that Vance-Owen has rewarded Croats with over a quarter of Bosnia. He hurries to sign. "[No interpretation] "[In English] The Vance-Owen plan places the mixed city of Mostar in a Croat province. The Croats have long coveted Mostar as their capital. They use the peace plan as the green light for a takeover but Vance-Owen also binds each province to protect ethnic minorities. The Croats appear not to notice. "[No interpretation] "[In English] May the 9th, 1993, the Croats mount an all-out assault in Mostar. The Bosnian forces resist. "Have you always seen Mostar as the capital of Herceg-Bosna? "Yes, all the time. "Even though it was a majority Muslim? "No, there are no majority in Mostar of any nation. Before the war, the equal number of inhabitants were Muslims and Croats. Difference was only few hundred. "But still you saw it as the capital of the Croatian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Yes, yes, it is. "Why? "Because this republic must have a capital. Must have one centre. Must have university. Must have other things which makes a republic a republic. Our own civilisation, level with theatre, symphonic orchestra, and so on. "But that civilised capital does not include Muslims. All the Muslims living on the west side are rounded up and forced across the river to the devastated east side. A brutal siege begins. Civilians become a weapon of war. "[No interpretation] "I saw a film where there was a night shot of people being driven out of West Mostar into East Mostar by HVO troops. "[No interpretation] "[In English] For four months, the HVO blocks all relief convoys to Muslim-held East Mostar, as the battle for the capital of Herceg-Bosna grinds on, Boban continues to starve civilians there. He is still using food as a weapon in his war. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Across the river, on the Croatian-held side of Mostar, there is no shortage of food. "Mostar don't have west bank, don't have east bank. Mostar is a unique town and I don't recognise this division. It's temporary front line but I'm an inhabitant of Mostar. Mostar is my native town and I don't want to divide it. "Other natives of West Mostar are busy sweeping away the last traces of their neighbours. Dispatches found some photographs among the ashes. "[No interpretation] "[In English] The Croats steadily work their way through the order of war pioneered by the Bosnian Serbs. In the Mostar region Muslim men of fighting age are herded off to camps such as Dretelj. Many had fought in the HVO. "[No interpretation] "[In English] On an island just off the Croatian mainland, victims from Dretelj are still held under police guard. Dispatches filmed there secretly. "It's important for you at the moment to go somewhere safe because your refugee status has only been extended for one month.
