"The government of Herceg-Bosna released these men only on condition that they would be sent abroad by the United Nations. They have left Bosnia forever. "It's important that you secure your safety first and foremost. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Throughout the war against Bosnian government forces, the regular Croatian army continues to pour into Bosnia to reinforce the HVO. This Croatian soldier was photographed on the front line of Mostar last June. "[No interpretation] "[In English] We have evidence of Croat army tanks in Ljubuski. "[No interpretation] "[In English] There is, and as I speak, a very substantial element of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, very substantial. And I must say I think it's an issue which the world ought to address more strongly. They addressed it in terms of the Serbs in the spring of 1992, with very considerable strength of purpose, but they have, to a great extent, ignored it in the last six months as it's built up. "President Tudjman's ambitions in Bosnia have been so ignored that in the Croatian capital of Zagreb it's business as usual. Croatia's backing of atrocities in Bosnia has gone unpunished. A senior diplomat told Dispatches the Croats have got away with murder, literally. At a European Community meeting in July ministers rejected sanctions. "Certainly that has been the view of the European Community, obviously influenced by the Federal Republic of German and other friends of Croatia, like Austria in the United Nations, Hungary and others and the United States. So the general feeling has been that it's better to make representations to President Tudjman and to criticise and to argue rather than to take action in terms of sanctions against Croatia. "We need an appropriate international approach to the Balkans, and until present time we have experienced many -- I mean many strange international politicians, genuinely losers in their own countries, like Lord Owen, Lord Carrington, lord that and that, and they were sent to this part of the earth to play an irresponsible political games. "One winner in these irresponsible political games has been Franjo Tudjman. In July he abandoned any pretense of supporting a unified Bosnia by calling openly for a carve-up. Peace negotiations are now based on a union of republics or mini-states. Tudjman has satisfied his obsession. Next on the agenda, the joining of this part of Bosnia with Croatia. "[No interpretation] "[In English] In Herceg-Bosna, in towns like Capljina, the new state is taking shape. The few factories are getting back to work. Children are getting used to a new curriculum, the same one taught in the Croatian motherland. But just outside Capljina, a convoy waits to collect the Croat refugees driven out from Central Bosnia. For these people, Tudjman and Boban's land grab has backfired. They come from outside Herceg-Bosna, where the HVO is losing more and more territory to Bosnian government forces. The Croats of Central Bosnia are now reduced to a few besieged pockets, falling one by one. The latest is Vares, where 20.000 people have fled. Mate Boban's only solution is to offer them a home in the barren land of Herceg-Bosna. "In Sarajevo, Croats face an uncertain future. 30.000 Croats live here. It's still the largest Croat city in Bosnia but the Herceg-Bosna government has abandoned them. Only the church is left to protect them. The spiritual leader of all Croats in Bosnia, Archbishop Vinko Puljic, refuses to leave his cathedral despite constant pressure to move to Herceg-Bosna. "[No interpretation] "[In English] Ivan Tomislav is a Croat citizen of Sarajevo. He feels betrayed by Mate Boban and his fellow Herzegovinans in Grude. "[No interpretation] "[In English] For the Croats in Sarajevo, Mate Boban's invitation to come and join other Croats in Herceg-Bosna is unacceptable. "[No interpretation] "[In English] This is a tragedy. And this tragedy could be attributed to the leadership of Mr. Tudjman because he has made many wrong decisions, and I mean he is simply, and his mentality is a mentality of a genuine loser. "[No interpretation] "[In English] The choice now facing Bosnian Croats is stark. For most it's Herceg-Bosna or nothing. Franjo Tudjman has carved out his chunk of rock in Bosnia. He's fulfilled his personal obsession with no international reprisals. But the price has been the betrayal of Bosnia and the sacrifice of his own people."

utterances.text: "Journalist: Okay, so if you just look at me. Could you tell me first about what happened this week when you became Prime Minister? Why did you become Prime Minister? "Jadranko Prlic: You must ask those persons who choose me. Now we have a new government of Herceg-Bosna with many new persons, and I think that this new government will be very good and this government has responsibility for all things in Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna. Now we have all ministry in our government and I think we are able to do good business. "Journalist: Before you were acting Prime Minister. Why have you now changed to become Prime Minister? "Jadranko Prlic: Before? Because we didn't be republic. We had been Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, as temporary organisation. Now according to Geneva agreement, we created a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I am the Prime Minister of this new government in new structure of Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, in future union of Republic of BH. "Journalist: And you've done that even though Geneva Agreement hasn't gone ahead, it hasn't been signed by all three parties? You still set up a government? "Jadranko Prlic: But all three parties accepted principles, this thing of principles, not border realign of -- excuse me, I made a mistake. All three parties accepted principle of organisation of future BH. "Journalist: You said when I asked you why you'd become Prime Minister, that depends on the people who chose you. Who did choose you? "Jadranko Prlic: Our parliament, parliament of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the president of Croatian Bosnia, according to law. "Journalist: And are they representative? Who did they represent, the Parliament? How were they elected? "Jadranko Prlic: All municipalities of Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, more than 30 municipalities in this parliament. This parliament has 70 members. "Journalist: And do they come from all over Bosnia? "Jadranko Prlic: Not all over Bosnia. All parts of Bosnia in which Croat lives. "Journalist: So you have representatives from Central Bosnia and from -- "Jadranko Prlic: From Central Bosnia, Northern Bosnia or Bosanska Posavina, Middle Bosnia, Herzegovina and -- "Journalist: Where is the seat of government? "Jadranko Prlic: Here in Mostar. "Journalist: Could you tell me that like in a statement here, Mostar is the seat of government, just it makes it easier. "Jadranko Prlic: Mostar is the seat of government all the time. "Journalist: And what is the division of responsibility between Mostar and Grude? Is there -- "Jadranko Prlic: There is no Grude in any document of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In all documents Mostar is the capital of Herceg-Bosna. "Journalist: And has that always been so? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: Why are you not all united here working together in Mostar? Why -- there seems to be two different administrations. "Jadranko Prlic: No, we have only one administration, but we have somebody, some ministries, all around Herceg-Bosna. "Journalist: So the president lives in Grude and the Prime Minister lives in Mostar. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. You may say it, it's true. "Journalist: Why would that be? "Jadranko Prlic: Because president lives in Grude. I live in Mostar all my life. "Journalist: One day, will the president come and live here, do you think? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: When do you think that will be? "Jadranko Prlic: Officially president of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, his seat is in Mostar, temporarily seated in Grude. "Journalist: Have you always seen Mostar as the capital of Herceg-Bosna? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes, all the time. "Journalist: Even though it was a majority Muslim? "Jadranko Prlic: No, there are no majority in Mostar, of any nation. Before the war an equal number of inhabitants were Muslims and Croats. Difference was only few hundred. "Journalist: But still you saw it as the capital of the Croatian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. Yes, it is. "Journalist: Why? "Jadranko Prlic: Because this republic must have a capital, must have one centre, must have university, must have other things which makes a republic as republic, around civilisation level, with theatre, with symphonic orchestra, and so on. "Journalist: Do you think the Muslims agreed with that at the beginning? "Jadranko Prlic: I think so. At the beginning, yes, but after that, when BH army became stronger and stronger, they choose their mind. "Journalist: Sorry, they did what? "Jadranko Prlic: They have choose their mind about it. "Journalist: They changed their mind. "Jadranko Prlic: They changed their mind. "Journalist: And what happened? Tell me what happened when they changed their mind. "Jadranko Prlic: You know, as in other part of Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, in one year before, there were more than 120.000 of refugees, of Muslim refugees, in this region. About 20.000 refugees in Mostar, 15.000 refugees in Travnik, and so on. And it was a very easy to manipulate with refugees. If you say to them you will stay in this flat, you will have job, you will have everything, because those person lose everything in their life, their old homes and so on. And it is very easy to manipulate with this population. It is one of the main problem in development, the process in BH, because almost all soldiers have been taken from this population. "Journalist: So can you tell me about how Mostar was saved from Serbs? What happened here in Mostar to repel the Serbs? "Jadranko Prlic: Liberated Mostar. It was more than one year ago, HVO liberated Mostar, because in this period, only military troops in Mostar was HVO. There was not BH army in this region. After liberalisation, Muslims created BH army. "Journalist: So did the Croats alone fight to -- "Jadranko Prlic: Not only Croats. Many Muslims fight in HVO. "Journalist: As part of HVO, they were part -- "Jadranko Prlic: Not as part, member of HVO. "Journalist: And let's say you empowered the Serbs and then Mostar was at peace. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: And then what happened? "Jadranko Prlic: Refugees, changing of politics, of Muslims and so on, is the real cause of conflict between Muslims and Croat in our region, because you know, if Croats want to ethnic cleansing, or to win Muslims, they might do at any moment, because we was much stronger than Muslims. We didn't want it. After BH army became stronger and stronger, they started fighting with Croats, and now we have result of this fighting. "Journalist: Do you think you could have repelled the Serbs without the Muslim soldiers in HVO? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes, yes. "Journalist: Without any Muslim soldiers. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes, we were able to do it. "Journalist: Why did you arm them? Why did you allow them to be part of HVO? "Jadranko Prlic: Because they want to be member of HVO. HVO in this period was voluntary army. "Journalist: So then you issued, as far as I understand, a declaration that they -- that all BH army soldiers should hand over their weapons on the 15th of April, is that right? Is that correct? "Jadranko Prlic: Excuse me, I didn't understand it. "Journalist: You said on the 15th of April that BH soldiers should give their weapons back to HVO. Is that correct? "Jadranko Prlic: I didn't understand you. "[No interpretation]. "Jadranko Prlic: No, did nothing. It's not correct, no. "Journalist: So what did happen? "Jadranko Prlic: Nothing. "Journalist: Why are you in this situation where you're fighting now? You were in alliance with these soldiers, now you're fighting against them. How did that happen? "Jadranko Prlic: Muslim army want to occupy all Mostar. It's only true. Because HVO had all, all town. Had everything in Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna. There was not BH army in this period. After that, Muslims became and create -- became creating new army, BH army, or Muslims Army. In first period it was BH army, now it's only the name. In reality, it is Muslims army. "Journalist: So they started the fighting in Mostar against Croats. "Jadranko Prlic: They started fighting in all Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. "Journalist: But in Mostar? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: It was the Muslims who started the fighting. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. It's official statement. "Journalist: And what did the HVO do when the fighting started? "Jadranko Prlic: Defend. Start defend. "Journalist: But why did you use Muslim troops if you didn't need them at all? Because at the beginning you fought side by side, you fought to defend your city. "Jadranko Prlic: No, we didn't use Muslim troops. We have Muslims in HVO. It was voluntary army and those Muslims want to be member of HVO. They are no any Muslim troop. "Journalist: So really you think the breakdown between Muslim and Croat troops happened only because the Muslims became aggressive, not -- "Jadranko Prlic: You know, Muslims wanted to find new territory for all Muslims. You know, many Muslims were pushed away from their territory by Serbs, and Muslims tried to get new territory. It was very hard task to do it against Serbs. It was easier to do with Croats. It's the main reason for this conflict. "Journalist: So what's happening now? You've got most of the west bank is Croat. What's happening in the east bank? Can you describe that to me? "Jadranko Prlic: No, Mostar don't have west bank, don't have east bank. Mostar is a unified town, and I don't recognise this division. It's temporary front line. But I'm an inhabitant of Mostar. Mostar is my native town. And I don't want to divide them -- to divide it. "Journalist: So what do you think will happen? Because at the moment you couldn't go to the east. I mean it is effectively a divided town, isn't it? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: So how -- "Jadranko Prlic: It is a temporary situation. I think that inhabitants of Mostar, Croat, Muslims and Serb, will overcome the situation in near future. "Journalist: How? "Jadranko Prlic: On political way. "Journalist: So you will have a united town again? You will have all the people on the east bank? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes, we will have united town with all other inhabitants; Croats, Muslims and Serbs. "Journalist: On what terms? What terms? What -- "Jadranko Prlic: I'm not sure. But I really believe it. "Journalist: And will you allow the BH army to have a part in Mostar as well? "Jadranko Prlic: No one army will have any part of Mostar. We don't need any army. "Journalist: Not even the HVO? "Jadranko Prlic: No one army. "Journalist: Can I ask you now about Central Bosnia, what is happening in Central Bosnia at the moment? "Jadranko Prlic: We have war in Central Bosnia between Croats and Muslims. Muslims army succeeded to occupied many towns in Central Bosnia, for instance, Travnik, Bugojno, Fojnica, in Northern Herzegovina Konjic and Jablanica, and in those towns, there are no Croats in this moment except [indiscernible]. Muslim finished ethnic cleansing of Croats in this region of BH. "Journalist: What is HVO doing at the moment for those areas? "Jadranko Prlic: Defend -- defend one -- two enclaves, no. HVO in this moment is in situation to defend three enclaves Middle Bosnia. Zepce second, Kiseljak part of Fojnica and Kresevo, and Vitez, Busovaca, part of Travnik and New Travnik. "Journalist: How are they doing? How is the strategy proceeding? Is it going well? "Jadranko Prlic: It is going not so good because we are in war but I think that we are able to defend this town, this municipality. "Journalist: Is that where HVO is now concentrating its effort in Central Bosnia? "Jadranko Prlic: It's probably problem of military strategy. I am not military man. I am just president of government. "Journalist: It seems to me that it was a strategy that was -- that was almost bound to fail, to try and get the whole of Central Bosnia. That it was too ambitious [indiscernible]. "Jadranko Prlic: No. We have only one ambition: To defend Croats in all BH. We don't want all BH or great part of BH. We want only one part of BH in which we have sovereignty in BH. And all other people who live in this part has the same right as Croat any other region with Serbian or Muslim majority. "Journalist: Going back to Mostar again, if all Muslims have rights here, why have so many Muslims left this part of Mostar? "Jadranko Prlic: I think that more Croats leave Mostar than Muslim. It's our evidence. "Journalist: And also talking about the HVO policy, Croat policy is to defend all Croats in Bosnia, the fact is that the people, the Croat people of Central Bosnia are being, as you said cleansed down. Is that not a rather unfortunate thing? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. It's very unfortunate thing, because we didn't prepare for war with Muslims. We tried to establish good cooperation with Muslims. You must know one thing: We gave [indiscernible] to Muslim, all the war. We gave them our house and anything else, refugees of Muslims. We constructed new road to Central Bosnia, through the mountains. Through this road all refugees, all Muslim refugees, went out from BH and all humanitarian aid now go through this road. We didn't want to fight Muslims. "Journalist: Were you in any way influenced by the peace plans? I mean the peace plans have changed since the beginning. What did you think, for instance, about Vance-Owen in the way that it treated Croats? "Jadranko Prlic: I think it was very good plan for all three sides in BH. I think that this plan was the best among all other plan. "Journalist: Why? "Jadranko Prlic: Because in this plan, BH will be state. Only Croats now in BH want BH state. Serbs and Muslims don't want BH. Serbs want Serbian Republic or Greater Serbia. Muslims want Muslim state. Only Croats want BH as a state. And I think that Vance-Owen plan has a guarantee to establish new state, decentralised state, and achieve all nationality in BH. "Journalist: Okay. So what do you think your policy, Croat policy, in BH has really achieved for Croats? What do you think that you have achieved for Croats? "Jadranko Prlic: We achieved one thing: Croats became factor in BH. We are not satisfied with the result of this war, but it's problem of other three nations, not Croats. You must know that before the war, in all population of BH, were only 17.6 Croats. Croats lives in many part of BH, from the north to the south. We don't have so huge concentration of Croat to establish some new state. We don't want Croat state in BH. It's it. "Journalist: But the people of Central Bosnia, as we've seen, from Vares and other places, are coming down, being made refugees. Do you not think that in some way you are responsible for that fact, that people -- that Croats are having to leave Central Bosnia? Do you not think you put so much effort into this area of Herceg-Bosna, into Herzegovina, that actually the people of Central Bosnia have been abandoned? "Jadranko Prlic: Vares is one Croat enclave in Central Bosnia with no communication with the main body of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Vares has only one very little [indiscernible] 1.000 soldiers. Front line between Croats and Muslims was about 60 kilometres. When Muslims concentrated so huge troops, two corps, it was obvious that Croats didn't have any chance to defend this town. It's the main reason for fail of Vares. "Journalist: Can we pause there for a minute. "Okay. I want to change slightly to find out some more details about things we were talking about at the beginning. Can you explain to me -- you said you've now become Prime Minister, which I understand. Are there any plans for elections in Herceg-Bosna? "Jadranko Prlic: Excuse me? "Journalist: Are there any plans to hold elections in Herceg-Bosna? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. We have plans for elections in Herceg-Bosna but in this period, it is not -- it is not real. We must wait the end of war. We must know which territory will be boundaries and so on, and after that, it may be -- excuse me -- after that, we will be able to organise election in Herceg-Bosna. Election in this period may be manipulated and may be not real, real result, because as you know, now we have more than 200.000 of refugees who are abroad. "Journalist: When the war comes to an end, can you -- can you see what sort of shape Herceg-Bosna will be where the territory will be, and the boundaries? "Jadranko Prlic: I think that politics negotiation will resolve this problem and Croat will be accept all solution. As you know Croat first accepted all plan from international community, and we are ready to do the same if this plan will be satisfying for Croat as a minimum, requesting. "Journalist: Did -- talking about plans, did the Vance-Owen plan have any influence over Croat policy? "Jadranko Prlic: As you know, Croat accepted this plan first, and I think it was some kind naive of Croats. Really they believed in this plan. But from the point of view of Muslims, it was only buying of time, prepare for war against Croats. It's one of cause of this conflict in BH. "Journalist: But in the Vance-Owen plan Croats got significantly more than their 17 per cent, didn't they? Why was that? "Jadranko Prlic: Croats didn't -- excuse me. Would you repeat once again? "Journalist: I just wondered what you thought about the fact that in the Vance-Owen plan, Croats got nearly, I think, 25 per cent. "Jadranko Prlic: Croats didn't get anything. Croats has it from the previous period, and it is not the true. This part of BH will be only provinces, and these provinces got all inhabitants, which lives in this territory, but not Croats. "Journalist: So it didn't have an influence in the provinces, that you began to think that the provinces you'd been allocated under Vance-Owen were Croat provinces which needed -- "Jadranko Prlic: These three provinces were with Croat majority. It's only true, nothing else. "Journalist: So no action was taken as a result of those provinces being given officially through the Vance-Owen plan? "Jadranko Prlic: No. We made a deal with Muslims to create new government in provinces and we elected candidates, as proposal, but Muslims didn't want to participate in this process. But you know that Izetbegovic signed the declaration with Croats about future constitution of these provinces. But as you know, Muslims didn't want to do it. "Journalist: Can I ask you about the structure of HVO? What is the HVO? "Jadranko Prlic: HVO, HVO, is the name of our army, Croatian Council of Defence. It is significant. We are Council of Defence, not of attack. And it's true during all war. "Journalist: What else does it do? Is it just involved in the military? "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: So it has no role in other part of the administration? "Jadranko Prlic: No. Role of HVO is the same as the role of any army in any state in the world. "Journalist: How is it financed? How do you pay for it? "Jadranko Prlic: From our fiscal system. We have customs, we have taxes, and so on, and we have enough money to finance the war. "Journalist: Not from a local based system? "Jadranko Prlic: Not from? "Journalist: Locals; each unit being financed locally? "Jadranko Prlic: You think municipal? "Journalist: Yes. "Jadranko Prlic: It's a part of all system, all financial system. "Journalist: Does each municipality have a control over their bit of the HVO? "Jadranko Prlic: No. We have central organisation of that. "Journalist: Where is that based? Where is the central organisation of the army? "Jadranko Prlic: Where is the headquarters? "Journalist: Yes. Where is it based? "Jadranko Prlic: Excuse me. In Citluk and Posusje. "Journalist: I wondered about how much help the Croatian army has given the HVO. "Jadranko Prlic: They are no of any help from the Croatian army from beginning of war except volunteers from Croat. You know that people from this region have been first volunteers in the war in Croatia, and after the beginning of war here, all of them came back to this region and started to defend this region. "Journalist: So there is nobody fighting here who is not from this region? "Jadranko Prlic: I think so. "Journalist: So what was the significance of the alliance announced between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic, the military alliance? What was the meaning of that alliance? "Jadranko Prlic: The meaning as any alliance. "Journalist: Can you explain that? "Jadranko Prlic: No. "Journalist: I think my last question at the moment is just can you tell me why -- what you felt about the bridge coming down? The Sanski Most, Stari Most, sorry. "Jadranko Prlic: I think it is terrible, and I think that the old bridge or Stari Most have been destroying more than one year and a half, and this week is final date of this destroying. Now we are going to [indiscernible] some activity for preparing documentation, planning, projecting and so on, and start activity to reconstruct this old bridge just after the end of there war. "Journalist: Why did it need to be destroyed, then? "Jadranko Prlic: I don't know. There are no any political and military reason to destroy this bridge. But destroying of this bridge is just to -- one evidence of the kind of this war, of dirty kind of this war, of anything, as you know, about the character of this war. "Journalist: It seems to me such a symbol of Mostar, being an ethnically mixed city. Do you see it as being the end of that possibility, that Muslims, Croats and Serbs can live together in Mostar? "Jadranko Prlic: No, no. I believe in some kind of joint living. We will live in the future in this region as neighbour. I believe good neighbour. "Journalist: Equal neighbours. "Jadranko Prlic: Yes. "Journalist: Even though this will be a Croat province and this will a Croat capital, you will be equal neighbours. "Jadranko Prlic: Equal. You may live in France as American without any problems. Do you have any problem in Paris or in Bonn, Amsterdam? No. You may live in this town. I think that all -- all inhabitants of Mostar must live in this Mostar. "Journalist: And they won't have any problems living here? "Jadranko Prlic: No. "Journalist: Finally, why -- can you just explain to me the decision to reopen the cafes yesterday? It seems to be -- "Jadranko Prlic: I didn't know. It's a decision of municipal, not central government. "Journalist: So it's nothing to do with you? "Jadranko Prlic: I think it is good cafe is open. "Journalist: Why is it good? "Jadranko Prlic: Because you may drink coffee. "Journalist: Okay. Can we pause there? I just want to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall also have a break now. It is now 25 minutes to 6. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have resumed our hearing. I've been informed about a personal problem regarding the witness. She has a child and must fly back after the hearing today, after 7.00. So we have an hour left. If we have not finished the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination today, the witness will have to come back on another day. I don't know where you stand, Mr. Mundis. Have you finished viewing the film?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if you have no further questions, the Defence team has one hour for its cross. The Prosecution has had an hour and a half, so you are half an hour short, Mr. Karnavas. I assume you are the person starting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. By agreement from -- well, it would be nice in the future if we know if there is a problem with the witness, so we could dispense with the formalities in the beginning. Maybe I should use this microphone, Mr. President, so if I could have just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My name is Michael Karnavas, I represent Jadranko Prlic, the gentleman that you interviewed. I'm going to try to hit some of the general areas and hopefully my colleagues will have enough time to go into more specifics. First I want to talk to you a little bit about this production of yours. You indicated -- you told us a little bit about your background and you indicated that normally, when you're an independent producer, you have to pitch the idea, right?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then I take it, in pitching the idea, you have a result in mind before you even pitch it?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I think you have an idea of the story, of course, but with a fast turn-around as I described - and a six weeks turn around for 40-minute film is a very fast turn-around - you go relatively unprepared. You go with what you have read in the newspapers and nothing else. You are not able to research too much in advance so you pick things up as you go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. Would it be fair to say that when you pitched the idea, the idea that you pitched was Greater Croatia, the carving up of a certain part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be annexed to Croatia? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it would fair to say that it was with that in mind that you went, later on, into the field in order to create this film?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could step back, as I understood you, you were under the impression at the time that this was a fast breaking story, so to speak. Those were your terms, by the way.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes. It was happening. I mean, I have to say, looking at the film, again, I had forgotten, I have to say, how much had already happened, how far down the road it already was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to stop you right there. So may I take that as an admission, somehow, that after looking at the film now, you see that part of your thesis was perhaps maybe wrong?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No, not at all. In fact, quite the reverse. I'd say looking at the film reminded me of what a powerful story and how convincing it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially when you take that footage and you zoom the camera into the flag with the Catholic church in the background, because you want to stress the point that here are these Croatian Catholics doing all these things to the Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I think I made it quite clear in my first piece of evidence that I wasn't arguing for, you know, the Muslims. I was arguing -- what the point that the film was trying to make was that there was a mini-state being carved out in Herzegovina in a very similar way to the way the Serbs had -- were trying to carve out their mini-state in Serb Republic, so I don't think that -- I don't like the idea that I was kind of special pleading for the Muslims. That was not my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that wasn't what I was suggesting, that you were pleading for one side or the other. What I am saying, however, is, and I put to you, that you went there with a result in mind, and your result in your mind was these Croats are -- from Croatia are, one, trying to establish a Croatian state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and secondly, the Croats from the Herzegovina area of Bosnia-Herzegovina were abandoning and sacrificing the Croats of Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It is correct. It wasn't a particular -- it's not a particularly original argument. It was the first time it had been put together on British television in that way but it was very well documented in the press, which was how I had got hold of the story in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you read the press, that gave you the idea, you pitched the idea, off you went into the field.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to us -- maybe I should slow down a little bit because even though I didn't have my coffee, usually I tend to rush these things. We speak the same language and the interpreters are going to yell at us fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Rightly so. So let's slow it down. So as I understand it, you were a history major?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: History and theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: History and theology. Is there a particular period? I mean history is a big picture, you know.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I guess I did 19th century British history, 17th century European history, and 13th century Anglo-Saxon history. I mean, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So fair to say not much on the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Not much on the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you didn't research, do any original research other than, say, reading the newspapers in order to pitch this particular idea?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We did have our document by that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Did you do any research, original research?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: What would you count as original research?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe getting not just one document but getting more. Maybe not just targeting one person or two people to interview but targeting many.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, we had spoken to Lord Owen, who I think put his views pretty firmly. We had spoken to journalists and politicians who were pretty shocked and horrified by what was going on in Zagreb. We had a couple of documents. We had -- I mean, you know, we -- we had enough evidence to persuade channel 4 to let us make the programme, and they are renowned for their journalistic, you know, acuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I wasn't aware of that, but let me ask you this: Did you do any research to see what the Cutileiro Plan was?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember what the Cutileiro Plan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what about did you look at any other -- did you look at the Vance-Owen Plan that was being proposed? Did you actually see it, study it?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We -- we did study it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "we," does that include you in that "we"?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Me and my colleague, Paulette Farsides, we studied it quite thoroughly. It seemed to me to have an instrumental effect on the whole -- what was going on, so it seemed necessary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what plan came after that one, the Vance-Owen Plan, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I certainly don't at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing a plan that came after that, any original documents?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we went and did the film about "The Serbs in the Corridor." I can't remember which plan was on the table. There were so many different plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, "The Serbs in the Corridor," that was much later, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: That was '94, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's much later. I mean, if you -- I mean, it stands to reason if you do a documentary on '93 and you're doing something in 1994, it stands to reason that what you saw in 1994 would not necessarily apply to what you did for 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No, but I mean I accumulated a body of knowledge over my working involvement with the region over four or five years, but it was ten years ago and I have different things to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Fair enough. Now, I look at number 11 in this statement that apparently you signed today. It's a one-page page and two paragraph statement. And from reading it, it would appear that you don't have your notes.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So there is nothing that I can look at or the honourable members of this Tribunal can look at to verify what exactly you're telling us; in other words, what documents you saw, who you attempted to interview, who you actually interviewed, who you included into your video, who you excluded in your video. We don't have any of those notes, do we?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No, we don't, but I remember very clearly who we interviewed, and they are all in the film. I cannot remember any that we kept out. I mean, in fact, you know, we had the three main protagonists. I think the lineup is -- I mean, I'm again rather kind of impressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, all right. Forgive me for not being as satisfied as you are, but we don't have your notes, that's the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't know what these notes are that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: -- I would have. I mean, I'm not a print journalist. I'm a television journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We cannot transmit anything unless actually we've recorded it. It's very difficult to include things like documents. They don't move, they don't talk, so therefore, our blood, our meat for making television programmes is the things that we record, and that's what you saw in the film. That is testament enough to the work that we did, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess what I wanted to see is your research, Madam, because you claim that you saw documents, and what I put to you is --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: The documents that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have no reason to believe you or to trust you when you say "I don't have any notes now." Where can you verify what documents of any of these previous agreements that you actually reviewed? If the answer is, no, you don't have it, I'll take it, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the documents I referred to are in the film, they are actually filmed in the film and highlighted in the film. If you want to review those, those are quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Notes -- do you have a notepad, a story board, something?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I have to say it would be nice if television were as programmed as you think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer is no. So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It didn't exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: -- so I don't quite know what you're looking for. It never existed. So this thing -- you know, you suggest that television journalists go out with a story pad. We don't have the time for a story that's happening so quickly in a war zone, where you're trying to piece things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just looking at what you say here. These are your words, "I have not been able to locate any of my notes."

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I assume you had notes to lose. Now you're telling me you never had any notes.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, the notes would have been, you know, How do we fly into Sarajevo? How do we get from Split to -- logistical notes. I don't think it's editorial notes that we are missing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about footage? We have the complete interview of Mr. Prlic. Did you interview, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We did. And he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you? Did you?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do we have all his footage?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: The BBC, I believe, have that footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Has that been turned over to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't know, but, I mean, if Mr. Prlic's interview is there, I can only assume that Mr. Boban's interview is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what about the -- did you interview President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I interviewed President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's the clip that we saw?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: There are various clips in the film, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But that's from your interview, not somebody else's interview?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Not somebody else's interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Where might that be, because I don't believe that we have that?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't know. I have to say I don't know, but it may be that the BBC has that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please slow down and make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the other fellows that you interviewed? Everybody in that film. Do you have any footage of any of those people other than the one that we have for Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't personally have any of that stuff, I'm afraid, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that because you sold it to -- or it's not part of your archive any more?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It's not part of my archive any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was sold to the BBC?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No. It was -- you know, you cannot afford to keep all archive rushes that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: So it was just destroyed, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what has happened to it. I gave it to channel 4, channel 4 will almost certainly have junked it after ten years after transmission. It is of no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So does that mean that that would go -- that would apply also for President Tudjman and also Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the fact that the -- Mr. Prlic's interview is in the possession of the Court, means that it is quite likely that the BBC also has Mate Boban's interview because I know they've used that in another context. It's also quite likely that they have the Tudjman interview for the same reasons, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever asked to find out?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And but with the other footage you believe it must have been junked.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it you shot quite a bit of footage. So what remains is what we have right now, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we don't have an unedited version of the various shots that you took, or the various interviews that you have.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who chose the editing? You know, which snippets? And I'm saying that because I noticed with Mr. Prlic you asked him specifically to say, Could you say it on the record, Mostar is the capital, because you're obviously looking for that one little punchline, and so could you tell us who did the editing?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: As I think I've already explained, it was my colleague and I who chose the particular pieces that went in, and another colleague who actually did the technical editing. So there is a distinction there, but the editorial line, the pieces of interview that were chosen, were my responsibility and my choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the people that you chose to interview, that list, who came up with that list, if you know, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I -- I mean, as I said, the film was made by myself and my colleague, Paulette Farsides. It would have been a collaborative enterprise. I cannot imagine how we actually came -- I mean, I cannot remember how we actually came up with the final list, but I mean, they were -- they were the kind of obvious people to interview, you know, the president of the state, the president of the mini-state, the newly appointed Prime Minister of the new state, and you know, political advisers who had been at Karadjordjevo, Owen he was at the peace plan and had a vision of that. I mean, it's kind of obvious where the list came from. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you didn't think it was necessary to interview anybody else. That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember whether there was anybody else that we wanted to interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How about Izetbegovic? Did you ever ask him, you know, President Izetbegovic, I want to interview you because I'm doing this film on Greater Croatia. Perhaps you could share with us your ideas on what's happening in all these negotiations you're doing? Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No. We didn't want to have Izetbegovic. Actually, since you mention it, I do remember that we interviewed -- I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not on the film?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: He's not in the film. He's a senior Bosnian in the Sarajevan government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you only had your notes, you see. That's why I'm asking for those notes because maybe your notes would reveal --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: But you have this notion of these notes that are kind of -- I can see, you know, wonderfully laid out. It's not like that on the road. It just ain't like that when you're in a war zone particularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, could you kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, especially when you have a result in mind and the focus. You have already written the story and now it's just a matter of trying to present it.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No. I think if you look at the cast of characters, we did interview -- he's called Ejup Ganic. That's who we interviewed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I think he was Prime Minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: The reason we really assembled the characters is, as I said at the beginning, we were making a film about the Croats. We weren't making a film about the Muslims and what was going on with them. That's why, if you look at the film, actually there are very few Muslims in it. It's about the Croats and what was happening to the Croats, both in terms of what was happening in Herzegovina and what that was doing to the other Croats in Bosnia, particularly in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, there were a lot of questions to Mr. Prlic regarding the HVO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I've just seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were a lot of questions as to why did you arm the Muslims? Did you hear yourself ask that question?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Because that's what he told me he had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- Well, he, he himself personally?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that in the film that he said that he armed the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah, at the beginning, when the relationship broke down, the Muslims and the Croats got together to defend Mostar and to defend that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How much of that did you know before you went there?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know when the Patriotic League was formed? Or better yet, who are the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what kind of relationship the Muslims of that area had with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It was however long ago it was -- 13 years ago. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And, well, did you ever ask around who might have been the commander of the Bosnian Muslims in that area to maybe interview him and try to find out what the conflict was?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, there were no Muslims in that area at that time. They had been fully cleansed. I'd been in that area in -- earlier in 1993 and I had met many Muslims then. There were no Muslims, as far as I could see, in Herzegovina except a few very, very frightened refugees living at the top of a school in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to make sure I heard this correctly. Your testimony today is that in Herzegovina, or Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were few Muslims living in that period when you took that film. That's your position?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, it was certainly the Muslims I had met six months earlier when I'd been in the area had all not -- were all not there any more. They had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is in?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: In Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Herzegovina. It's a pretty large place.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It is a large place. I mean, there were Muslims on the east bank of Mostar. I went to interview them, as you saw in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there any army there, any Muslim army there on the east side? Yes, no, maybe.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: There probably were but it was extremely dangerous and I wasn't going to risk my life any more than I already was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that wasn't the question, was it?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whether it was dangerous or whether it was peaceful. I'm asking you was there an army there of Muslims? If yes, did you interview them?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever ask the question, is there anybody here on this side that I might be able to talk to in order to get sort of like a -- how about a novel idea, a balanced picture?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: We interviewed two soldiers who had fought with -- three soldiers, actually, who are in the film who had fought with the HVO, who were Muslims, and now were part of the Muslim army in Sarajevo. It was far too dangerous to interview people on the front line at Mostar. It was the most dangerous front line I think in the whole of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that -- you had indicated to us that this was a very complicated story. Those were your words. You know, initially during your direct examination, when you were pitching the idea. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you interviewed Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Stjepan Kljuic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you ask him, by any chance, what his involvement was in 1991 and 1992 in the party, in the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's not in the film, so I guess whatever he said probably was edited out, if he did say anything about that. Did he by any chance share with you the positions that he expressed and others expressed on the 27th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of any activities going on at that particular time - I'm talking about the end of 1991, or even sort of the middle of 1991 onwards - with respect to how the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina were trying to resolve the Croatian issue within this whole conflict that was going on as a result of the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to hit some high points so others can question you. Did you ever go to Central Bosnia to meet any of the folks over there, whether they were the Muslims or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I never went to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So for me to ask you a bunch of questions about Central Bosnia would be futile.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Pretty futile, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yet you had reached already the conclusion that these folks, the Croats, at least, of Central Bosnia were being sacrificed for the creation of a -- of Herceg-Bosna which was in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I think the evidence, the testimony of Archbishop Puljic in Sarajevo represents, you know, the -- the whole feeling of Croats in Bosnia. You know, that -- one inevitably has to be expedient if you're making these films. You're doing it on a very tight turnaround, on a very tight budget. As I said, in a war zone you have to make decisions about what you can and can't do. I think that Puljic said what we needed him to say to back up our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you said that he -- that Puljic had said that they were trying to get him -- to convince him to leave Sarajevo. You're shaking your head. I take it that's a yes.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Give the translators a break a little bit. Now, what I'm wondering is, I looked at this film and I don't see anywhere where where Puljic is saying that they are trying to convince him to leave Sarajevo. I mean, it wasn't in the film. Maybe I missed it. And I watched it several times.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I thought he said it in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe -- I know that he was concerned that he wanted all of Croatians of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be included in some sort of a negotiated plan but I didn't get the impression that he directly said, and His Honours have the video, that they were trying to move him out of Sarajevo and have him come to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I thought he said that quite clearly in the film, that he wasn't going to leave his cathedral in Sarajevo because that's where he felt he could represent the -- you know, all the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just the Herzegovinan Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference between him not wanting to leave and him being told or urged to leave there, don't you think? There is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: There is definitely a distinction but I really cannot remember at this distance what he precisely said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I know that he went on record many times after. I wasn't the only person he went on record to. He was -- he publicised his campaign extremely fully. He was a staunch anti-Herceg-Bosna person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. As were many other Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: It seemed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, depends on where they were.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And but did you -- I guess I keep coming back to this idea - I'm trying to figure out - did you do any research to know what was happening in 1991 and 1992 in the region; in Herceg-Bosna, Herzegovina, Central Bosnia? Did you have a sense of what was really happening before jumping into or fast forwarding to that particular period where you thought this was a breaking story? I guess that's what I'm wondering.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, I'd been there, as I said, for quite a long time in the spring of 1993. I know, you know, it had -- the conflict had antecedents far beyond that. I think I had read extremely fully and thoroughly, not only historical records but, you know, the material that was coming out from '90, earlier onwards. I think I felt that I was fully abreast of all the evidence in order to make that film. I needed to be. It was, as you have repeated, a complicated story, and to extract the main story out of it, you needed to be that well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you indicated on there that Dispatch was able to obtain the signed, secret protocol.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then there was that -- sort of looked like History Channel a little bit. Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: History Channel wasn't invented then, I don't think, so maybe it came afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe it was the result of the BBC's effort in covering the war.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you say secret. This was not known to the public?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Until you revealed it. Take a stab; yes, no, maybe.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: What do you mean by the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say secret. Secret means nobody knows about it other than the people that were sitting around, making this sort of signed secret protocol. This was '91, November 1991. So by 1993 you're saying you obtained this.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes. We obtained it from some Croatian journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I don't think they had published it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But to your mind, this was a secret document?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you look at, by any chance, any other documents that came after that? For instance, the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, otherwise known as HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever try to figure out what was this Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, I think I tried to figure it out in the film. I think the conclusion I came to is in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What is the difference between HZ HB and HR HB?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: One is the Croatian Community and one is the Croatian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, could you tell me what the difference is between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Do you know when the HR HB was established; the republic, that is?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I -- I probably knew at one point but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That would have been around August 28th, 1993. And in the film, Mr. Prlic tries to describe to you as to -- that they have this new government, right?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you make the point or you ask him the question that he was acting Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you if I were to tell you - and the Prosecution can correct me if I'm wrong - that he was never an acting Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, as you saw in the whole interview, there was a language problem. But I think what I understood from Mr. Prlic was that he had been acting Prime Minister and that he'd been promoted to being Prime Minister, but maybe that was to do with the language problem. Mine as much as his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, you assume because somebody told you that he had been an acting Prime Minister, he had been president of, you know, of the government, you know, during -- when it was Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you thought that he was actually an acting Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: My impression is that he actually said that in the tape, but I mean, I -- maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you make any different -- in your mind did you make a distinction as to this -- this Croatian Community versus the Croatian Republic?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now he says in -- he says during the interview, that he -- when it was a Croatian Community, that it was -- that it was temporary.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you ever ask him -- or better yet, since we know the answer is no, why didn't you ask him, What did you mean by "temporary"? What exactly was this all about?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Well, again, if you looked at that tape as we just did, I think the communication wasn't particularly strong between me and Mr. Prlic. I think, with the benefit of hindsight, it would have been better if we had done it in his language and we could have actually had a proper debate going. As it was, I don't think there was much room to ask really detailed questions about what was going on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: -- because his English wasn't up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but were you in control of the interview, so -- I mean -- we can't blame Mr. Prlic now.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I'm not blaming him at all. I'm saying with the benefit of hindsight we could have got more information, probably, out of him if we had conducted it in his language rather than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But suffice it to say he was open?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you didn't have to cut through any red tape to see him?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. He was very -- I remember him being very helpful indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. He wasn't trying to steer you in the wrong direction or hide anything?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were no, for instance, boundaries --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- you know, to start with?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it -- I wasn't there so I wouldn't know, but I take it there wasn't anything off the record, on the record?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because it seems to me you're not the off-the-record type.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: You're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. Because we are running out of time and hopefully we can conclude your cross-examination and have you home so you won't have to come back, at this point in time, I'm going to yield the floor to my colleagues, and I thank you very much. I hope I didn't press you too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next Defence counsel, please. We have half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Giles. My name is Peter Murphy, I represent Mr. Stojic. I just have a couple of questions for you. You said that you wrote the script for this film.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you write the script before or after visiting the area?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: That would have been the final stage of the whole process. It would have been done about the day of transmission, so it was after, well after, visiting the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: When you approached channel 4 with the story, you clearly had in mind that it was going to be about the setting up of a mini-state.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: About what you called, I think, in the script the carve-up of part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that once you had got channel 4 to agree to that, that was going to be the story and that was going to stay the story?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I think channel 4's reputation as the sort of seat of best journalism would not have allowed me to get away with that. If I'd gone out there and found a very different story, I would have come back with a very, very different story. As it was, I came back with the story I had. And what I thought I had read about was in fact fully justified when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You came back with the story you expected to come back with, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember at this stage. I think -- I think it was far stronger than any of us had thought it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Of the film footage that we saw, was all of that shot by your photographer, Mr. Baily?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No it wasn't. There was quite a lot of archive shots, particularly of the fighting. And the shots in Dretelj were not shot by me. Dretelj was closed by the time I got there, although when we went to Badija and saw the refugees who were being shipped out to third countries, that was all my footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Maybe you can't help, but as a percentage, what amount of the footage would you think was shot by Mr. Baily during your visit?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I would say between 85 and 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. And just one other thing: I was intrigued by one answer you gave at page 82, line 13, for the record. You said that you wouldn't want to interview President Izetbegovic. Is that because you didn't think he would have anything to add to the story?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember, to be honest, why we didn't, but I think -- I come back to this thing that it was really a Croat story and therefore, in a way, his part, I mean, his part wasn't very major. It didn't seem to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: There was a scene where you showed him, I think, with President Tudjman, signing --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Signing the agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But despite that, you didn't think he would have anything to add if you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No. The main story was really the Zagreb Herceg-Bosna relationship, and that -- you know, we had President Tudjman, seemed to me that we had some pretty heavy hitters. We didn't need Izetbegovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Giles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, I'm going to take up just five minutes, and my colleague has asked for three minutes. Mr. Praljak has asked for three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm the Defence counsel for the accused General Praljak here, and I just have a few short questions for you. At the beginning of your film and during your direct testimony you spoke about the country Bosna, called Bosnia, and you visited Bosnia, you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: If you mean I was using a shorthand and not saying Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes, yes, that's what I referred to it as.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as you just said, that shorthand name was placed in the footage which you showed to the British public; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you know what that country, Bosnia, was called before the war, before that unfortunate war in 1992 and 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I believe it was called Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you really think that?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the fact that Yugoslavia was a federation made up of six independent autonomous republics?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of those republics of the former federation?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was its name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I'm sure I did at the time. I was very immersed in the subject. I'm not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know today what the country was called while you were visiting in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I've just said I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know then, at the time?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what that country is called today?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: No. I don't think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't, right. There is part of the interview, a small portion of your conversation with Lord Owen, and he mentions the presence of the Croatian army, the army of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia. I want to ask you this: While you were working on this broadcast, this programme, did you ever see yourself elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well, actually. In Siroki Brijeg we saw quite a lot of tanks and I remember putting the question to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was when?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: In November, 1993, when we were there shooting the film we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, you gave the Prosecution a brief statement. I'm going to read it out to you, just one of the things you say. It is paragraph 4 and 5. You said that you were in Mostar in November, 1993, and then the next point, in point 5, you stated that you were there at the HVO press office in West Mostar, and so on and so forth. And that you remember having met there a colleague journalist, Ed Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was in November, 1993, was it?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that Ed Vulliamy testified here just two or three days ago and in his statement, for the record - I have to quote the exact page - it was on the 9th of May, on page 10, line 15, of Mr. Vulliamy's testimony, where he claims he was in Mostar on the 7th and 8th of September, 1993, that that was when he was in Mostar. And then on page 17, line 23, up until page 18, line 4, Ed Vulliamy, Witness Vulliamy, stated that he was there from September, 1993 -- or rather, from September, 1993, until mid-February, 1994, he was not in Mostar. So something is not quite correct there. Either you have made the mistake or Mr. Vulliamy has made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: As I think I hope I've made clear in my testimony, this was all a long time ago. I have left the subject of Bosnia-Herzegovina and indeed the whole of former Yugoslavia behind. I have a new career. It may be that I misremembered it, although I would question -- I -- I would like to stick by my story that I remember him being in the HVO press office that day when I went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But if I put it to you that in the statement you gave to the Prosecution on the 6th of April 2006, and the 15th of May 2006, that is to say this morning, you were very definite. There were no reservations there; you say in November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I still -- I know when I was there. I was there in November, 1993. I remember Ed Vulliamy being there. If I've got that wrong, I apologise. I'm not retracting it. I'm saying, however, that it was a long time ago and that a lot of this has become very, very foggy in my mind because I'm no longer intimately involved with any aspects of anything to do with the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the footage with Lord Owen and the conversation there with him, it would emerge from what he said, from his statement -- or rather, an introductory question first of all. Did you personally talk to Lord Owen --

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- in the film?

utterances.speaker: BELINDA GILES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did, right.
